extracted.intended_audience: citizens, lawmakers, and constitutional designers/readers interested in republican constitutional structure
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and criteria for structuring a republican constitution to preserve liberty: how to prevent departmental encroachments, secure checks and balances, set qualifications and terms, and protect minority rights in a federal system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasional appeals to the people
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitutional road to the decision of the people ought to be marked out and kept open for certain great and extraordinary occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep an appeal to the people available for exceptional circumstances, but not as a routine remedy. Objections: does not help if two departments combine against the third; frequent appeals imply a defect in government; they may disturb public tranquillity and substitute public passion for reason. Use only for rare, extraordinary cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic appeals to the people are ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodical appeals are nearly as ineligible as appeals on particular occasions; distant periods produce weak restraint and recent abuses may have completed their mischief before remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constitutional designs that mandate regular/periodic popular revisions (e.g., fixed-term conventions) because: remote censures are a feeble restraint; abuses can become entrenched; historical example (Pennsylvania Council of Censors) showed partisanship and inefficacy. Periodic revision risks the same defects as frequent appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not appoint reviewers who were involved in the period reviewed
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluding from revision assemblies persons concerned with the government during the period would be intended to ensure impartiality, but the experiment suggests this is difficult to achieve in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting reviewers who recently served in, or were active in, the branches under review invites partisanship. Even attempting to exclude them may produce less-qualified assemblies elected under party auspices. The Pennsylvania example shows such bodies split into fixed parties and decisions governed by passion rather than reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior structure must supply checks and balances
rubrics_metrics.description: Where exterior provisions fail, the defect must be supplied by contriving the interior structure of government so that its constituent parts, by their mutual relations, keep each other in their proper places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design government offices and relationships so that each part can check the others; rely on institutional design (not frequent appeals) to maintain constitutional partition of power. Examples: different modes of appointment, division of the legislature, and constitutional means for defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each department should have a will of its own; minimize cross-appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Each department should be so constituted that the members of each should have as little agency as possible in the appointment of the members of the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize channels of influence between appointment processes of different branches to preserve distinct interests and reduce capture. Recognize some deviations (esp. for judiciary) may be necessary for practical reasons, but preserve as much separation as practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Members' emoluments must be independent
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of each department should be as little dependent as possible on those of the others for the emoluments annexed to their offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure salaries and financial emoluments are insulated from other branches' control so independence is real not merely nominal; dependence on another branch for pay undermines independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design judiciary appointments to secure qualifications and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Peculiar qualifications being essential in the judiciary, the primary consideration ought to be to select that mode of choice which best secures these qualifications; permanent tenure will soon destroy dependence on appointing authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance selecting qualified judges with insulating them from political pressures: choose appointment mechanisms that secure competence; recognize that life/permanent tenure reduces accountability to the appointing authority and thus supports judicial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide the legislature into different branches
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedy for legislative predominance is to divide the legislature into different branches, and render them by different modes of election and different principles of action as little connected with each other as the nature of their functions will admit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fragment legislative power (bicameralism, different electorates, differing term lengths) so that ambition and local interests check each legislative branch and reduce the risk of concentration of power in a single assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortify the executive against legislative predominance
rubrics_metrics.description: As the weight of the legislative authority requires division, the weakness of the executive may require that it be fortified; an absolute negative on the legislature may be neither safe nor sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the executive with constitutional means (not necessarily an unchecked veto) and qualified connections (e.g., links to a weaker legislative branch) so it can defend its constitutional rights without enabling abuse. Avoid relying solely on an absolute negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition must be made to counteract ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: The great security against a gradual concentration of the several powers consists in giving administrators the necessary constitutional means and personal motives to resist encroachments of the others: 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie private interest to public office rights (division of offices, differing local ties, personal motives) so each actor's self-interest helps preserve constitutional balance. Use rival interests and institutional design as 'auxiliary precautions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Federalism creates double security
rubrics_metrics.description: In a compound republic power surrendered by the people is first divided between two governments and then subdivided among departments; hence a double security arises to the rights of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple levels of government (national and state) plus internal departmental checks so different governments control each other and also are self-checking. Federal structure reduces danger of majority oppression and provides additional restraints on usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of interests protects minority rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard one part of society against the injustice of the other by comprehending in the society so many separate descriptions of citizens that an unjust combination of a majority of the whole will be improbable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage a variety of interests, classes, and sects across an extended territory so majority coalitions based on narrow interests are unlikely. Security for civil and religious rights depends on multiplicity of interests and sects and the extent of the country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix suffrage and representative qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Electors for the House of Representatives are to be the same as electors of the most numerous branch of the State legislatures; representatives must be 25 years old, seven years a citizen, an inhabitant of the state, and hold no office under the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixing these qualifications in the constitution preserves a uniform standard and prevents state governments from altering the federal electoral basis; these reasonable limitations keep the door open to merit across conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use frequent elections to secure dependence (biennial recommended)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent elections are the policy by which dependence and intimate sympathy with the people are effectually secured; biennial elections under the federal system cannot possibly be dangerous to requisite dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select election frequencies so representatives remain responsive to constituents but not so short as to undermine governance; historical examples (British triennial/septennial, colonial practice) support biennial elections as appropriate for the House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match term length to extent of delegated power
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the power is greater, the shorter ought to be its duration; conversely, the smaller the power, the more safely may its duration be protracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose term lengths inversely proportional to the scope of authority: bodies with more concentrated power should face more frequent accountability; more limited bodies may have longer terms consistent with their restraint by other institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frequent references that inflame public passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent appeals to the people would carry an implication of some defect in the government and would, in great measure, deprive the government of that veneration which time bestows; the passions, not the reason, of the public would sit in judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design constitutional remedies that limit exposure to transient popular passions. Recognize that popular decisions are often colored by pre-existing party attachments, prominent personalities, and passions that may subvert reasoned assessment of constitutional questions.
